gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a PC power supply's hold-up time is specified at full load: ATX 3.1 requires 12 ms at 100% load and recommends 17 ms at 80% load. Measured that way, the power stations rated at 10 ms or faster (EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, BLUETTI Elite 300) fall inside even the minimum. Ratings of 15 ms (Elite 200 V2) or 'under 20 ms' (Jackery v2 line) are longer than the ATX 3.1 full-load minimum, so they only work when the PSU does better than spec or runs well below full load.
standout_why: ChatGPT ran no searches and cited no pages, so there is no rival page to compare against. Its answer says 20–30 ms 'can cause the PC to shut down' and suggests '10 ms or less', but it never gives the PSU-side spec or the load it is measured at. It also doesn't say that no power station maker states a load for its switchover rating, while the ATX figure is tied to a load (100% / 80%). Our current page mentions 'ATX 3.1's 12 ms floor' in one note but not the full-load condition, the 17 ms at 80% recommendation, the ATX 3.0 to 3.1 change, or a measured PSU hold-up figure. The new part is the normalisation table: switchover rating vs PSU hold-up at a stated load.
decides: It supports the 10 ms-or-faster group (DELTA 3 Plus, which StorageReview measured at just over 8 ms; C1000 Gen 2; Elite 300) as the picks for a gaming PC, because their ratings are below the 12 ms minimum a compliant ATX 3.1 PSU must reach even at 100% load. It moves Elite 200 V2 (15 ms) and the Jackery v2 line (under 20 ms) to 'only if your PSU does better than spec'. HWBusters measured 20.2 ms on one 850 W ATX 3.1 unit, but its AC-loss-to-PWR_OK time was 16.5 ms, so even that example is tight against 20 ms. It also adds a second normalisation footnote: in UPS mode the C1000 Gen 2 load limit is its 1,800 W bypass, not its 2,000 W inverter rating. Elite 200 V2 shares 1,800 W between charging and bypass. Neither limit matters for a 500–700 W gaming PC.

findings.label: PSU hold-up time requirement, ATX 3.0 vs ATX 3.1
findings.value: ATX 3.0: 17 ms at full load. ATX 3.1: 12 ms at full load (required), 17 ms at 80% load (recommended)
findings.source_title: Seasonic: Differences Between ATX 3.0 and ATX 3.1 Standards
findings.note: Seasonic says ATX 3.1 relaxed the requirement 'from 17ms at full load to 12ms at full load' and recommends '17ms at 80% load'. This is the PSU side of the comparison. Power station switchover ratings have to be compared against this figure at its stated load.

findings.label: Measured PSU hold-up, one ATX 3.1 850 W unit (Gigabyte AE850PM PG5)
findings.value: 20.2 ms hold-up at full load; 16.5 ms AC loss to PWR_OK
findings.source_title: HWBusters: Gigabyte AE850PM PG5 850W ATX v3.1 PSU review, Hold Up Time
findings.note: HWBusters: 'comfortably exceeding the ATX 3.1 requirement of 12ms at full load'. They call the 16.5 ms PWR_OK time 'just below the usual 17ms target' and give no load for that figure. This is one sample and not representative of all PSUs. It shows a real PSU can exceed 20 ms on output, but its power-good signal can drop sooner.

findings.label: UPS switchover (maker) and UPS-mode load limit
findings.value: UPS 10 ms ('under 10 ms UPS switchover'); AC output 2,000 W (3,000 W peak); AC bypass 1,800 W max; AC charging 1,200 W, 1,600 W UltraFast
findings.note: No load condition or footnote on the 10 ms figure. In UPS mode the load runs through the bypass, so the usable limit is 1,800 W, not 2,000 W. That is still far above a 500–700 W gaming PC. The page showed no price.

findings.label: UPS switchover: rated vs measured
findings.value: Rated <10 ms (spec table) / measured just over 8 ms
findings.note: Measured with a Quarch Mains Power Analysis Module on 'a workstation'. The review gives no wattage for the load. This is the only measured figure in the group, and it is below the 12 ms ATX 3.1 full-load minimum.
